strengths: The paper presents a clear and interesting insight: self-attention in text-to-image diffusion models appears to contain transient instance-boundary structure, and the proposed IEP/ABDiv mechanism is a plausible way to extract it.
TRACE is positioned well against important problems in unsupervised instance segmentation and weakly supervised panoptic segmentation, where instance separation is a real bottleneck.

The experimental section is fairly broad: results are reported on VOC, COCO 2014/2017, and additional appendix benchmarks, with improvements over MaskCut, ProMerge, CutLER-style pipelines, and tag-supervised panoptic baselines.

The ablations support the main design choices: semantic-timestep attention alone gives little gain, IEP+ABDiv improves results, and one-step distillation greatly reduces inference latency while improving edge connectivity.
The method is practically useful as a plug-in refinement module for existing segmentation pipelines, and the qualitative examples make the boundary-separation behavior easy to understand.
weaknesses: The central claim that diffusion models are 'annotation-free' or provide an unbiased alternative is somewhat overstated. Large text-to-image diffusion backbones are trained on massive image-text corpora likely containing benchmark-like data and strong semantic supervision through captions; this complicates comparison to genuinely unsupervised methods.

The weakly supervised panoptic comparisons are not always clean. Some headline claims compare tag-supervised TRACE variants with different backbones or stronger pretrained components against point-supervised baselines, making it hard to isolate the benefit of the proposed instance edges from backbone and pretraining scale.

Absolute unsupervised instance segmentation AP remains low despite large relative gains, especially on COCO/LVIS/SA-1B. The paper could better calibrate practical significance rather than emphasizing percentage improvements.

Several implementation details are underspecified for reproducibility: exact attention layers used, resolution/memory handling for HW-by-HW attention maps, LoRA training schedule, edge decoder architecture details, threshold sensitivity, and BGP hyperparameters are only partially described.

The ablation that distillation improves substantially over the non-distilled teacher signal raises questions. More analysis is needed to show whether gains come from learning true instance boundaries, smoothing/postprocessing, dataset-specific fine-tuning, or implicit supervision from ImageNet-scale training.

The evaluation would be stronger with direct boundary-quality metrics against ground-truth instance boundaries, failure case analysis, and robustness tests on out-of-distribution images, crowded scenes, small objects, and domains far from diffusion pretraining data.

Computational cost is significant: training takes 8-10 days on A100-scale hardware and SD3.5-L requires substantial VRAM. The paper's 'lightweight' framing is true for the final decoder pass but less true for the overall recipe.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: obtaining instance-level cues without dense masks, points, or boxes for unsupervised instance segmentation and weakly supervised panoptic segmentation.
The core observation that diffusion self-attention at particular denoising timesteps can expose instance boundary structure is interesting and potentially useful.

TRACE is a simple and interpretable pipeline: select an Instance Emergence Point, compute attention boundary divergence, distill the result into a one-step edge predictor, and use the edge map to refine downstream masks.

The empirical section is reasonably broad, including UIS results on VOC/COCO, weakly supervised panoptic segmentation, ablations of IEP/ABDiv/distillation, backbone comparisons, conventional edge detector comparisons, and additional datasets in the appendix.

The reported gains over MaskCut/ProMerge-style UIS baselines are sizable in relative terms, and the qualitative examples support the claim that TRACE can help separate adjacent same-class instances and reconnect fragmented masks.
weaknesses: The main claims are stronger than the evidence. The paper repeatedly suggests that TRACE surpasses point-supervised panoptic methods using only tags, but the comparison is not clean: the strongest results rely on larger backbones, while same-backbone gains are mixed, especially on COCO where the ResNet-50 TRACE variant remains below EPLD.

Fairness of comparisons is a major concern. TRACE uses large text-to-image diffusion backbones such as SD3.5-L, substantial pretraining, ImageNet fine-tuning for the distilled edge predictor, and a downstream Mask2Former training pipeline. It is therefore unclear how much of the gain comes from the proposed attention-boundary idea rather than backbone scale, pretraining data, or extra training machinery.

The method is more supervised/trained than the framing suggests. Although it avoids instance annotations, the distilled edge model is trained on pseudo-edges generated from diffusion attention, often after fine-tuning on ImageNet. The term annotation-free is technically plausible but somewhat misleading as a practical comparison against training-free UIS methods.

Absolute UIS performance remains low despite relative improvements, e.g. COCO AP around 8 for training-free settings. This limits the practical significance of the method as an instance segmentation system, even if it is useful as a refinement cue.

The technical contribution is heuristic. IEP, ABDiv thresholding with mean plus/minus standard deviation, BGP propagation, and IoU-based merging are plausible but not deeply justified. The paper gives empirical ablations but little principled analysis of when these choices should work or fail.

The ablations are incomplete for the strength of the claims. The paper does not sufficiently isolate the contribution of diffusion backbone fine-tuning, ImageNet training data, edge decoder architecture, LoRA rank, thresholding rules, BGP hyperparameters, resolution, or alternative fixed timesteps chosen without per-image IEP.

The diffusion-versus-non-diffusion comparison is not fully convincing. Non-diffusion backbones are evaluated by applying ABDiv/BGP to them, but these models were not designed for the same latent attention behavior; this may create an unfair setup that favors diffusion models rather than proving the claimed hidden instance-edge prior.

The paper under-discusses failure modes. It does not adequately analyze crowded scenes, thin structures, occlusions, transparent/reflective objects, severe texture edges, small objects, stuff/thing ambiguity, or cases where diffusion priors hallucinate boundaries inconsistent with the image.
Computational cost remains significant. Training takes 8-10 days and SD3.5-L uses 32GB VRAM, which weakens the claim of practical scalability despite the one-step distilled inference speed.

Reproducibility is only partially convincing. The paper says code is in supplementary material, but key details such as exact prompts/null conditioning behavior, hook locations, layer selection, preprocessing, thresholding, training schedule, and baseline reproduction choices are either deferred or underspecified in the main text.

The writing tends to overstate novelty and impact. Prior work has already explored diffusion attention for segmentation and boundary/edge priors for weak supervision; the paper should more carefully position TRACE as a useful adaptation and refinement method rather than a broad replacement for instance-level annotation.

strengths: Clear and interesting central insight: the paper identifies a transient instance-boundary signal in diffusion self-attention and turns it into a practical segmentation prior through IEP, ABDiv, and one-step distillation.

The empirical evaluation is broad and convincing overall, covering unsupervised instance segmentation, weakly supervised panoptic segmentation, multiple datasets, multiple baselines, component ablations, similarity metrics, diffusion/non-diffusion backbones, and conventional edge detector alternatives.

The method is well motivated by concrete failure modes of existing UIS pipelines, especially adjacent instance merging and single-instance fragmentation, and the qualitative examples support the boundary-centric framing.

The one-step distillation is important practically: it reduces the expensive per-image diffusion analysis to a fast predictor and makes the approach more usable than a purely inversion-based pipeline.

Results are strong relative to the relevant weak/unsupervised baselines, including consistent gains on COCO/VOC and competitive tag-supervised panoptic performance that can surpass point-supervised methods in the reported settings.
The paper is generally clear, with useful algorithmic descriptions and a reproducibility statement indicating code and full pipelines are included in the supplementary material.
weaknesses: Some claims are stronger than the evidence warrants. The framing of TRACE as fully annotation-free should be nuanced, since the diffusion backbone is trained on large-scale image-text data and the panoptic setting still relies on image-level tag-supervised semantic models and downstream Mask2Former training.

Fairness of some comparisons is not completely airtight: TRACE uses very large diffusion backbones such as SD3.5-L, while several baselines use smaller or different model classes; compute and pretraining scale may explain part of the advantage.

Although relative UIS gains are large, absolute AP values remain quite low on challenging datasets, so the practical quality of the unsupervised instance masks is still limited outside downstream refinement settings.

Several implementation details are underspecified or deferred: BGP is described at a high level, many hyperparameters are inherited from baselines, and the exact training data/protocol for the distilled edge decoder and pseudo-edge generation could be more explicit for independent reproduction.

The ablations support the main components but leave some questions open, such as sensitivity to thresholding choices for ternary edge labels, LoRA rank/backbone fine-tuning choices, prompt/null-text variants, and robustness across domains very different from diffusion pretraining data.

The paper occasionally overstates novelty or generality, for example suggesting diffusion models “secretly function as instance edge annotators” and that TRACE surpasses box-/point-supervised alternatives, when the result depends on particular benchmarks, backbones, and downstream pipelines.

strengths: The core idea is original and interesting: the paper identifies a transient instance-structure regime in diffusion self-attention and turns it into annotation-free instance boundary cues via IEP and ABDiv.

The method is technically coherent and modular: pseudo-edge extraction, uncertainty masking, one-step self-distillation, and boundary-guided propagation are well motivated and can plug into several downstream segmentation pipelines.
The empirical scope is broad, covering unsupervised instance segmentation, weakly supervised panoptic segmentation, edge-quality evaluation, backbone comparisons, ablations, and cross-dataset tests.
Ablations support several design choices, including the importance of IEP over fixed semantic timesteps, KL over simpler metrics, uncertainty masking, and the limited role of decoder capacity.
The paper is unusually explicit about limitations, including failures on tiny satellite objects and out-of-distribution medical imagery.
weaknesses: Several headline claims are overstated or depend on comparison choices. In particular, claims about surpassing point-supervised panoptic methods are sensitive to backbone differences, reproduced-versus-reported numbers, and whether the comparison is made against ResNet-50 or Swin-L variants.

The evaluation mixes multiple settings: training-free UIS, fine-tuned UIS, tag-supervised panoptic segmentation, SAM seeding, and open-vocabulary segmentation. This breadth is valuable, but it sometimes obscures exactly what supervision, backbone capacity, and training data each comparison uses.

The method relies on very large pretrained diffusion backbones and substantial distillation cost, e.g. multi-day ImageNet fine-tuning and high VRAM. This weakens the practical “scalable annotation-free” framing unless code, checkpoints, and detailed compute budgets are released.

The theoretical analysis of IEP is suggestive but rests on strong simplifying assumptions, such as time-invariant clean similarities and a monotone inverse-temperature view of attention dynamics. It does not fully explain why real diffusion self-attention should satisfy these assumptions.

Absolute AP values for unsupervised instance segmentation remain low on challenging datasets despite relative gains, so the practical impact for standalone annotation-free segmentation is more limited than some of the framing suggests.

Reproducibility details are incomplete for a method with many moving parts: exact hook locations, attention aggregation choices, LoRA targets, pseudo-label generation scale, downstream hyperparameters, and checkpoint availability would be crucial for independent verification.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: obtaining instance-level boundary cues without dense instance annotations, with applications to unsupervised instance segmentation and weakly supervised panoptic segmentation.

The core observation that diffusion self-attention contains transient instance-boundary information is interesting, and the IEP plus ABDiv pipeline is a plausible and conceptually clean way to extract it.

The empirical scope is broad: the paper evaluates on VOC, COCO, additional UIS datasets, open-vocabulary segmentation settings, multiple diffusion/non-diffusion backbones, and includes several ablations.
The method appears practically useful as a refinement module for weak or unsupervised segmentation pipelines, with clear gains over MaskCut/ProMerge-style baselines in the reported tables.
The paper includes failure cases on satellite and medical imagery, which is helpful and more candid than many submissions in this area.
weaknesses: The claims are often stronger than the evidence. In particular, statements such as diffusion models “secretly function as instance edge annotators” and “annotation-free” instance segmentation are overstated given the reliance on large pretrained generative models, ImageNet-scale fine-tuning, pseudo-label distillation, and downstream segmentation pipelines.

The comparison to point-supervised panoptic methods is not fully convincing. Some headline claims mix different backbones and capacities, e.g. tag-supervised TRACE with Swin-L versus point-supervised ResNet-50 or older baselines, making it hard to attribute improvements to TRACE rather than stronger semantic models/backbones.

The absolute unsupervised instance segmentation performance remains quite low despite large relative gains, e.g. COCO AP values around 8 to 13. This limits the practical significance of the UIS results and should temper the paper’s conclusions.

The instance-edge evaluation is concerning and needs much more scrutiny. TRACE reports extremely high ODS/OIS against COCO-derived instance boundaries compared with conventional edge detectors, but the construction, thresholding, tolerance, train/evaluation separation, and possible pipeline bias are not explained enough to make this result fully credible.

The method is computationally heavy despite the one-step decoder: training requires 8 to 10 days and 20 to 32 GB VRAM with very large diffusion backbones. The paper presents this as minimal overhead, but the cost and deployment constraints are substantial for many users.

The theoretical justification for IEP is weak relative to the real system. The analysis assumes time-invariant clean similarities and a simplified softmax temperature trajectory, which does not faithfully model changing diffusion representations or multi-layer attention aggregation.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Many details are deferred to inherited baselines or described only at a high level, including exact prompts/null conditioning, attention layer choices, LoRA targets, training data usage, pseudo-edge generation protocol, BGP implementation details, and hyperparameters for downstream systems.

Several baselines are not ideally matched. The paper should compare against stronger or more direct alternatives for boundary-guided segmentation, diffusion-feature segmentation, SAM-based mask generation, and recent open-vocabulary/weakly supervised panoptic pipelines under controlled backbone and supervision settings.

The paper’s framing sometimes blurs whether TRACE is an edge detector, a pseudo-label generator, a refinement module, or a component in a larger training pipeline. This makes the contribution harder to assess cleanly and risks attributing downstream gains entirely to the proposed edge cue.
The limitations are meaningful, not minor: the method degrades in tiny-object and out-of-domain medical settings, suggesting the diffusion prior is less general than the main narrative implies.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and timely idea: diffusion self-attention contains recoverable instance-boundary structure, and the proposed IEP plus ABDiv pipeline is a plausible and useful way to extract it.

The empirical evaluation is broad and convincing overall, covering unsupervised instance segmentation, tag-supervised panoptic segmentation, instance-edge quality, open-vocabulary segmentation, multiple diffusion backbones, and several datasets.

The reported gains are substantial in the main settings: TRACE improves UIS baselines by roughly 4-5 AP on COCO/VOC and enables tag-supervised panoptic segmentation to match or exceed point-supervised methods in several comparisons.

The ablations are stronger than average: component ablations, KL versus alternative metrics, decoder capacity, uncertainty masking, diffusion versus non-diffusion backbones, and conventional edge-detector replacements all support the core design choices.
The paper is unusually transparent about limitations, including clear negative results on satellite tiny-object datasets and medical histopathology images.
The method is modular and practically useful as a boundary prior that can be attached to existing segmentation pipelines rather than requiring a completely new segmentation model.
weaknesses: The novelty is meaningful but somewhat incremental relative to the growing body of work repurposing diffusion attention for segmentation; the paper’s main advance is specifically instance-edge extraction and distillation rather than a fundamentally new learning paradigm.

Some headline claims such as “annotation-free” require careful qualification: TRACE relies on large pretrained text-to-image diffusion models, ImageNet fine-tuning for the distilled edge generator in some experiments, and image-level tags for the panoptic setting.

The absolute UIS numbers remain low despite strong relative gains, especially on difficult datasets such as LVIS, KITTI, Objects365, and SA-1B, so the practical standalone quality of unsupervised instance segmentation is still limited.
The computational footprint is significant: training with SDXL/SD3.5-L takes 8-10 days and uses 20-32 GB VRAM, which weakens the framing of TRACE as lightweight despite fast distilled inference.

The paper would benefit from more detailed reproducibility information, including exact training schedules, data used for distillation in each setting, hyperparameters for BGP, thresholding, and whether all checkpoints/code will be released.

Several comparisons mix supervision levels, backbones, and pipeline components, making the strongest claims against point-supervised or open-vocabulary methods somewhat hard to attribute cleanly to the proposed boundary extraction alone.

The edge-quality benchmark is constructed from COCO panoptic masks and is well motivated, but it may favor methods designed to match panoptic instance boundaries; additional independent boundary benchmarks or human boundary studies would strengthen the evidence.
